Wave Properties.intro: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Understanding the properties and types of waves is essential for all of P6.

sections.title: Types of Wave
points: Transverse waves — oscillation perpendicular to direction of travel; e.g. light, water, seismic S-waves
Longitudinal waves — oscillation parallel to direction of travel; e.g. sound, seismic P-waves; have compressions and rarefactions

sections.title: Wave Properties
points: Amplitude — maximum displacement from equilibrium (m)
Wavelength (λ) — distance from one point to the next identical point (m)
Frequency (f) — number of complete waves per second (Hz)
Time period (T) — time for one complete wave: T = 1/f (s)
Wave speed (v) — speed at which wave travels (m/s)

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: v = f × λ (Wave speed = frequency × wavelength). Units: v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m.

keyTerms.def: Maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position
Distance between two adjacent points in phase on a wave
Number of complete wave cycles per second — measured in hertz (Hz)
Wave where oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
Wave where oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer

examTips: v = fλ — the most important wave equation. Rearrange to find f or λ.
T = 1/f — period and frequency are inversely related.
Amplitude affects intensity/loudness; frequency affects pitch (sound) or colour (light).
commonMistakes: Confusing amplitude (maximum displacement) with wavelength (distance between peaks).
clozePassages: Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — examples include light and water waves. Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer — sound waves are longitudinal. All waves have amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and wave speed. The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is speed, f is frequency, and λ is wavelength.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement from the rest position. A larger amplitude means more energy is being transferred. The wavelength is the distance between successive crests or compressions. The frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Period is the time for one complete wave. Frequency and period are related by: f = 1/T.

The wave equation v = fλ relates wave speed, frequency, and wavelength. If frequency increases and speed remains constant, wavelength decreases. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s). Sound travels much more slowly — about 340 m/s in air. Waves can be reflected, refracted, diffracted, and can show interference. These behaviours are explained by the wave model.

Reflection and Refraction.intro: Waves change direction when they reflect off surfaces or refract as they change speed at a boundary. These phenomena are key to how lenses, mirrors and optical fibres work.

sections.title: Reflection
points: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from normal)
Normal = line perpendicular to surface at point of incidence
Specular reflection: smooth surface (e.g. mirror) — parallel rays stay parallel
Diffuse reflection: rough surface — parallel rays scatter in all directions

sections.title: Refraction
points: Waves change speed when crossing a boundary between media
Change in speed → change in wavelength → change in direction
Light bends TOWARDS normal when entering denser medium (slows down)
Light bends AWAY from normal when entering less dense medium (speeds up)

sections.title: Total Internal Reflection
points: When light hits a boundary at angle greater than critical angle → no refraction, all reflected
Used in: optical fibres (communications, endoscopes), periscopes, binoculars
Only occurs when light travels from denser to less dense medium

keyTerms.def: A line perpendicular to a surface at the point where a ray hits
Angle between incoming ray and the normal
Change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary due to change in speed
Complete reflection at a boundary when the angle exceeds the critical angle
The angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs

examTips: All angles measured from the NORMAL, not the surface.
Refraction: towards normal = slower (denser). Away from normal = faster (less dense).
Total internal reflection requires: denser to less dense medium AND angle > critical angle.
commonMistakes: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal.
Saying refraction changes frequency — it changes speed and wavelength but NOT frequency.
clozePassages: Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface). Smooth surfaces produce regular (specular) reflection; rough surfaces produce diffuse reflection. Mirrors use regular reflection. The image in a plane mirror is virtual, upright, laterally inverted, and the same size as the object.

Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another with a different speed. When light passes from air to glass, it slows down and bends towards the normal. When passing from glass to air, it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The greater the change in speed, the greater the angle of refraction. Refraction explains why objects appear displaced when viewed through water or glass.

Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle. The light is completely reflected back into the denser medium. This principle is used in optical fibres — light travels along the fibre by repeated total internal reflection. Optical fibres are used in telecommunications to transmit data at high speed over long distances, and in medicine for endoscopes.

Sound.intro: Sound is a longitudinal wave that requires a medium to travel through. Understanding its properties and how it is heard is required for P6.

sections.title: Nature of Sound
points: Longitudinal wave — compressions and rarefactions
Requires a medium to travel — cannot travel through a vacuum
Speed in air: ~340 m/s; faster in liquids and solids (particles closer together)
Frequency determines pitch; amplitude determines loudness

sections.title: Hearing Range
points: Human hearing range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz
Ultrasound: above 20,000 Hz — used in medical scanning (foetal imaging), sonar, industrial cleaning
Infrasound: below 20 Hz — used by some animals; detected at large distances

sections.title: Echoes and Sonar
points: Echo = sound wave reflected from a surface
Sonar: time for echo to return → calculate distance (d = v × t/2)
Used to measure ocean depth and locate submarines

keyTerms.def: Longitudinal pressure wave — requires a medium to travel
Sound with frequency above 20,000 Hz — above human hearing range
Reflection of a sound wave from a surface

examTips: Sound is longitudinal; light is transverse.
Speed of sound in air ≈ 340 m/s. Sound travels faster in denser materials.
Ultrasound: f > 20,000 Hz. Infrasound: f < 20 Hz.
commonMistakes: Saying sound travels faster in less dense materials — it's the opposite.
clozePassages: Sound is a longitudinal wave caused by vibrating objects. It travels as alternating regions of high pressure (compressions) and low pressure (rarefactions) through a medium. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to vibrate. The speed of sound is approximately 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids, and fastest in solids. Sound waves can be reflected as echoes and refracted at boundaries between media.

The frequency of a sound wave determines its pitch. High frequency sounds have high pitch. The typical range of human hearing is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound; sounds above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound. Ultrasound is used in medical imaging, sonar, and measuring distances. The amplitude of a sound wave determines its loudness — a larger amplitude means a louder sound and more energy.

Ultrasound has frequencies above the upper limit of human hearing (20,000 Hz). It is used in medicine for prenatal scanning — ultrasound pulses are sent into the body and reflected at boundaries between tissues. The reflected pulses are detected and used to build up an image. Ultrasound is safer than X-rays for imaging soft tissue. It is also used in sonar to map the sea floor, and in industrial applications to detect cracks in materials.

Electromagnetic Spectrum.intro: The electromagnetic spectrum is a family of transverse waves that all travel at the speed of light in a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength.

sections.title: The EM Spectrum
points: All EM waves: travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; are transverse; can travel through a vacuum
In order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength):
Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma

sections.title: Uses
points: Radio waves: TV, radio, communications
Microwaves: satellite communications, cooking
Infrared: thermal imaging, remote controls, optical fibres
Visible light: vision, photography
UV: sterilisation, detecting forged banknotes, sunbeds
X-rays: medical imaging, airport security
Gamma: medical treatment (cancer), sterilising medical equipment

sections.title: Hazards
points: UV: skin cancer, eye damage (increases with frequency)
X-rays: ionising — cancer risk; minimised by lead shielding
Gamma: most ionising — highest cancer risk; controlled use in medicine

keyTerms.def: Family of transverse waves ranging from radio waves to gamma rays
3 × 10⁸ m/s — the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum

examTips: All EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy = more ionising.
Radio ROY G BIV Gamma — remember the order.
commonMistakes: Saying radio waves are the most energetic — gamma rays are.
Forgetting that all EM waves travel at the same speed in vacuum.
clozePassages: The electromagnetic spectrum is a family of transverse waves that all travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s). In order of increasing frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength and more energy. All electromagnetic waves can be reflected, refracted, and diffracted, and can travel through a vacuum.

Radio waves are used for communication — broadcasting, TV, and mobile phones. Microwaves are used for satellite communication and cooking. Infrared radiation is emitted by warm objects and used in remote controls and thermal imaging. Ultraviolet radiation from the sun causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer. X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, making them useful for medical imaging. Gamma rays are used to sterilise medical equipment and treat cancer.

Different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum interact with matter in different ways. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can damage living cells, causing mutations and cancer. Ultraviolet radiation can cause skin cancer by damaging DNA. Infrared radiation is felt as heat. Microwaves can heat water molecules in food. Radio waves are non-ionising and pose no known health risk at normal exposure levels. The ozone layer protects Earth from most harmful ultraviolet radiation.

Black Body Radiation.intro: All objects absorb and emit radiation. The balance between these processes determines an object's temperature.

sections.title: Absorbing and Emitting Radiation
points: All objects absorb and emit infrared radiation
Temperature constant: rate of absorption = rate of emission
If absorbing more than emitting: temperature rises
If emitting more than absorbing: temperature falls

sections.title: Black Body Radiation
points: A perfect black body absorbs ALL incident radiation (none reflected)
A perfect black body emits maximum radiation for its temperature
The Sun behaves approximately as a black body
Hotter objects: emit more radiation AND at shorter wavelengths (higher frequency)

callout.label: Energy Balance
callout.text: Earth's temperature is stable when energy absorbed from the Sun = energy emitted by Earth. Greenhouse gases reduce emission → temperature rises to establish new balance.

keyTerms.def: A perfect absorber and emitter of radiation — absorbs all incident radiation
Electromagnetic waves emitted by all objects due to their temperature

examTips: Temperature is stable when absorption rate = emission rate.
Hotter objects emit more radiation at shorter wavelengths.
Greenhouse effect: gases absorb Earth's infrared → reduce emission → temperature rises.
commonMistakes: Saying black objects always absorb radiation — this is about black bodies (theoretical perfect absorbers), not the colour black.
Forgetting that all objects emit infrared — not just hot ones.
clozePassages: All objects emit electromagnetic radiation — the hotter the object, the more radiation it emits and the higher the frequency of the peak emission. A black body is an ideal absorber and emitter of radiation. It absorbs all radiation that falls on it and emits the maximum possible radiation at each wavelength for its temperature. The Sun behaves approximately like a black body at about 5500°C and emits most strongly in the visible part of the spectrum.

The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun and also emits radiation. The balance between absorbed and emitted radiation determines Earth's temperature. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb some of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, warming the planet. Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations trap more radiation, causing the Earth's average temperature to rise — this is the enhanced greenhouse effect.

The intensity and wavelength distribution of radiation emitted by a body depends only on its temperature. As temperature increases, the peak of the emission shifts to shorter wavelengths (higher frequencies). This is why objects glow red, then orange, then white as they get hotter. The concept of black body radiation was crucial in developing quantum theory — classical physics could not explain the observed emission spectrum, leading Planck to propose that energy is emitted in discrete packets called quanta.
